Abstract Background  Achievement emotions play an important role in learning, significantly affecting well-being, learning satisfaction, and academic achievement, yet their application to healthcare education remains sparse. To address this gap, this study adapted the Achievement Emotions Questionnaire– Short Version (AEQ-S) in healthcare education. The objective is to assess the applicability, demonstrate its application, and guide future research in achievement emotions within this field. Methods  This study involved 296 pre-service students enrolled in interprofessional education (IPE) from various disciplines, including Chinese Medicine, Engineering, Law, Medicine, Nursing, Pharmacy, Speech and Hearing Sciences, and Social Work, who completed the adapted AEQ-S in IPE context (AEQ-SIPE) before and after the IPE. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and multiple linear regression were employed to examine the acceptability of AEQ-S. Results  The 32-item AEQ-SIPE capturing eight emotions (hope, pride, enjoyment, anxiety, anger, shame, boredom, and hopelessness) yielded good model fit: CFI = 0.937, NFI = 0.904, IFI = 0.937, TLI = 0.928, RMSEA = 0.076) and high internal reliability (α = 0.90 to 0.96). Regression analyses indicated that the eight emotions accounted for a significant amount of variance in explaining well-being and achievement outcomes. Pride positively predicted satisfaction in life, positive affect, and learning satisfaction, while shame negatively predicted satisfaction in life but positively predicted positive and negative affect. Conclusion  This study highlights the critical importance of achievement emotions in healthcare education and confirms the AEQ-SIPE as a valid tool for exploring these emotions in IPE. It sets the stage for future research to further investigate and understand the role of achievement emotions in this context.

Introduction Theory and empirical data have established the link between students’ emotions in the classroom (e.g., enjoy­ ment, anxiety) and their achievement outcomes. In par­ ticular, evidence has shown that students who experience positive emotions achieve better, enjoy social relation­ ships, and even live longer [1]. Defined as “emotions tied directly to achievement activities or achievement out­ comes” [2, p.317], this construct is referred to as achieve­ ment emotion (AE), which has been linked with various important learning outcomes such as motivation [3], engagement [4], learning persistence [5], satisfaction [6], problem-solving ability [7], and learning and achieve­ ment [8]. These established relationships may be why the repeated calls made to explore non-cognitive constructs to account for factors in explaining students’ engagement and achievement in healthcare education [9]. However, despite such calls to action, AE studies in healthcare edu­ cation settings remain scant, and actionable plans for inducing adaptive emotions appear not to be in place (cf [10, 11, 12]).

One way to draw traction on this important construct is by providing researchers with psychometrically sound measures and guiding them in conceptualizing impor­ tant studies to advance academic emotion theory and application in healthcare education. The Achievement Emotions Questionnaire (AEQ) is a widely-known multidimensional tool and is considered one of the seminal research measures on students’ emotional experiences in educational settings [13]. Framed using the control-value theory of achievement emotion [14, 15], this theory pos­ its that achievement emotions arise from the interplay between control (students’ perceived ability to influence academic outcomes) and value (the perceived impor­ tance of the achievement situation). The AEQ operation­ alizes this theoretical framework by assessing students’ AEs underpinning three positive (pride, hope, and enjoy­ ment) and five negative emotions (anxiety, boredom, anger, shame, and hopelessness). Each emotion reflects specific control-value combinations (e.g., anxiety devel­ ops when students highly value performance but per­ ceive limited control over success) that impact learning outcomes and well-being in healthcare education set­ tings [13]. It has been translated into various language versions, including Japanese [16], Spanish [17], Chinese [18], German [19] and Korean [20]. From the original 80 items [13], an AEQ-Short Version (AEQ-S) has been formulated, requiring less time to administer and score [21, 22]. AEQ has also been applied in various contexts: sports [23], physics learning [24], mathematics educa­ tion [25], language learning [26], and teacher education

[27]. However, healthcare education environments pres­ ent distinctive characteristics that may intensify achieve­ ment emotions beyond these traditional academic and professional training settings, including direct patient care responsibilities, exposure to human suffering and mortality, ethical decision-making under pressure, and the professional obligation to maintain competence where errors have life-threatening consequences. These unique contextual factors create heightened emotional stakes and may influence the manifestation and inten­ sity of achievement emotions differently compared to other educational domains. Previous studies suggest that students often experience a wide spectrum of emotions throughout their learning processes [28], and these emo­ tions affect achievement gains [14] and satisfaction [20]. These learning-related emotions may recur periodically at various frequencies in various learning areas, including healthcare education [11, 12]. Studies have shown that positive emotions (e.g., pride, hope) are associated with higher satisfaction and well-being [29, 30]. Conversely, negative emotion, such as shame, arises from negative self-assessments, often triggered by perceived failures or shortcomings. It is typically linked to decreased life satisfaction and increased negative affect, as shame pro­ motes feelings of inadequacy and self-consciousness [31]. A study found that in Belgium, the prevalence of anger, boredom, anxiety, and shame was 15.6%, 7.2%, 4.7%, and 4.5%, respectively [32]. In Hong Kong, more than 50% of the 1,119 undergraduate students who were polled reported having anxiety symptoms [33]. From the lens of the control-value theory of academic emotion, these emotions are linked with students’ well-being [34], satis­ faction [35], and even academic performance in the long term [14]. Despite all these significances, the validation and application of AEQ-S in healthcare education, espe­ cially in Interprofessional education (IPE) context, are unexplored areas with significant potential for learning outcomes.

An adaptation and application of AEQ-S to healthcare education, particularly in IPE, is an important step that will eventually lead to the development of a research agenda to understand the mechanisms within which AEs translate into achievement gains. IPE is fast becoming one of the accreditation standards for healthcare pro­ fessions because of the relative benefits of a team-based interprofessional approach to care management. Accord­ ing to the World Health Organization [36], promoting IPE from the onset of healthcare education encourages adaptability and prepares students to meet complex healthcare needs more effectively. By situating our study within a Ten-Day IPE Programme, we aim to capture the various students’ AEs experienced and investigate their correlations with well-being and learning satisfaction.

The present study Although the AEQ-S is a well-established questionnaire, its application in the context of healthcare is still very limited. Therefore, the purpose of this study was three­ fold. First, we wanted to adapt the AEQ-S for estimating students’ AEs by adapting the items to the IPE context. Second, we aimed to conduct a confirmatory factor analy­ sis using the advantages of within-network approaches in examining construct validity. Finally, we sought to estab­ lish the relationship between AEs as measured by the AEQ-S in the IPE context (AEQ-SIPE) and other theo­ retically relevant constructs such as well-being (indexed by life satisfaction, positive and negative affect) and learning satisfaction. In this study, we hypothesized that the various AEs they feel across the period of complet­ ing the IPE activities with diverse discipline memberships would be linked with their well-being (satisfaction in life, positive affect, negative affect) and learning satisfaction (team learning satisfaction). The inclusion of positive affect and negative affect is grounded in the circumplex model of affect [40], which defines emotional experiences

along dimensions of valence and arousal. This framework complements Pekrun’s Control-Value Theory of Achieve­ ment Emotions [2], as positive affect and negative affect capture broader emotional tendencies that shape the like­ lihood of experiencing specific achievement emotions (e.g., enjoyment, anxiety). The study seeks to answer the following question: How do achievement emotions, as measured by the AEQ-SIPE, relate to well-being and learning satisfaction in the context of IPE among health­ care students? Finally, we propose research topics using the newly validated scale to help plan new directions for IPE research.

Method Participants and procedures There were 296 students from two institutions of higher learning participated in this study. The participants were from eight disciplines: Chinese Medicine (n = 16), Engi­ neering (n = 2), Law (n = 15), Medicine (n = 110), Nursing (n = 107), Pharmacy (n = 24), Speech and Hearing Sci­ ences (n = 4), and Social Work (n = 18). There were 43.2% males and 56.8% females, with an average age of 21.68 years (SD = 2.11).

Students participated in a required credit-bearing “Ten-Day Interprofessional Education” programme on COVID-19 Infection Control and Management (Fig. 1). The IPE programme integrates team-based and casebased learning pedagogies to enhance collaborative lead­ ership, problem-solving, conflict resolution, and clinical

Adaptation of achievement emotions questionnaire in IPE (AEQ-SIPE) Content experts in the IPE were asked to independently review the items of the proposed scale conducted in Eng­ lish for content validity based on the original scale pub­ lished by Pekrun et al. [41]. For example, “I enjoy being in class” was slightly modified to “I enjoy being in IPE” making it more context-specific. Due caution was exer­ cised in the context adaptation process, where our pri­ mary goal was to maintain the conceptual meaning of the items. Furthermore, we calculated internal consistency reliability using Cronbach’s alpha and split-half reliability coefficient. To validate the scales, we examined withinand between-network construct validity.

Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted for within-network validation, and linear regression between the scales and external measures was used for betweennetwork validation, which functions similarly to criterion validity. Within-network construct validation is an exam­ ination of the factor structure, while the between-net­ work or external construct validation approach examines the relationships between the measures being validated and theoretical constructs [42]. We built from the litera­ ture and hypothesized that students’ AEs would be linked with their well-being (satisfaction with life, positive affect, negative affect). That is, students’ enjoyment (collected at

Time 1) will predict subsequent positive affect (collected at Time 2). CFA is part of structural equation modeling techniques, which enables the investigation of causal relations among latent and observed variables when the a priori model is specified [43]. This dual approach to scale validation has been popularly employed in validation studies and is thought to be robust [44]. It has also been used in healthcare education (e.g [45]).

Instruments Achievement Emotions Questionnaire - Short version in IPE (AEQ-SIPE). This study adapted the Achieve­ ment Emotions Questionnaire– short version [21]. The scale consists of 32 items divided into 8 subscales of 4 items each in the English version: enjoyment (4 items, “I enjoy participating so much in IPE that I get energized”; α = 0.96; split-half reliability coefficient = 0.94), hope (4 items, “I am full of hope”; α = 0.92; split-half reliability coefficient = 0.91), pride (4 items, “I am proud of myself”; α = 0.92; split-half reliability coefficient = 0.90), anger (4 items, “I am angry”; α = 0.94; split-half reliability coef­ ficient = 0.94), anxiety (4 items, “I feel nervous in IPE”; α = 0.90; split-half reliability coefficient = 0.87), shame (4 items, “I get embarrassed”; α = 0.95; split-half reliability coefficient = 0.95), hopelessness (4 items, “I feel hopeless”; α = 0.96; split-half reliability coefficient = 0.95), boredom (4 items, “I get bored”; α = 0.95; split-half reliability coef­ ficient = 0.94). To adapt the scale to IPE, the wording was slightly modified. For instance, the item “I enjoy being in class” was modified to “I enjoy being in IPE” (Appendix A). The scale is answerable from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

Life Satisfaction Scale (LSS) and Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS- Short Form). We used these scales to measure students’ well-being, which was used in a previous study among Asian students [46]. Life sat­ isfaction was assessed using the Life Satisfaction Scale (5 items; e.g., “In most ways, my life is close to my ideal”, α = 0.95) from Diener et al. [47]. The response scale ranges from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). We also used the 10-item PANAS-Short Form, developed by MacKinnon et al. [48], to measure positive and nega­ tive affect. Participants were asked to score their feel­ ings of positive (e.g., “Interested”; α = 0.94) and negative (e.g., “Afraid”; α = 0.93) affect on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree).

Learning Satisfaction with Team Experience. We uti­ lized the subscale of the Students’ Team Experience Questionnaire to measure learning satisfaction with team experience [49]. This subscale is composed of five items (e.g., “I have found working as part of an IPE team in my classes to be a valuable experience”; α = 0.94), answerable from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

Statistical analysis To establish within-network validity, we first conducted CFA using the Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation method to examine the internal structure (within-net­ work construct validity) of the AEQ-SIPE using health­ care students’ data, which determined if our data would adequately fit the eight-factor structure [50]. Eight achievement emotions (e.g., enjoyment and anger, etc.) were conceptualized as latent variables, each represented by four observed indicators. We ensured the distribution normality of these indicators before applying ML esti­ mation, which is noted for its robustness and efficiency. Additionally, error covariances were introduced between closely related indicators (e.g., enjoyment and anger) to account for shared method-specific variance and improve model fit.We used the standard goodness-of-fit indices such as the root mean square error of approxima­ tion (RMSEA), standardized root means square residual (SRMR), comparative fit index (CFI), normed fit index (NFI), incremental fit index (IFI), and the Tucker-Lewis index (TLI) in evaluating the model fit. According to guidelines, all indices must be more than or equal to 0.90, except for RMSEA and SRMR, which must be less than or equal to 0.08 [51, 52, 53]. To further understand the data, we used an independent sample t-test to examine gender differences and multi-group CFA to check for measure­ ment invariance between genders using nested mod­ els [54]. In the nested models (configural model, metric model, and scalar model), we imposed constraints gradu­ ally. First, we used configural model which contains the same factor structure with fixed and free loadings calcu­ lated concurrently in the groups, but parameter estima­ tions were not subject to any between-groups restrictions

[55]. Then, we tested for measurement equivalence under the metric model by demanding that the factor structure and factor loadings be equivalent in the groups [56]. To further assess measurement equivalence using the sca­ lar model, a restriction is that the factor structure and loadings, covariance and variance should be equal in the groups [57].

To achieve the purpose of between-network valid­ ity, we used multiple regression analysis to clarify the relationship between each of the four dependent vari­ ables and the eight independent variables (the AEs). We used Statistical Package for Social Sciences for the t-test and regression (SPSS Version 27; [58]) and Analysis for Moment Structures for the CFA (AMOS 26; [59]).

The eight-factor model was tested for gender-specific invariance. As we executed multi-group CFA, we gradu­ ally restricted the models and computed the CFI decrease among the models (i.e., metric model, scalar model, and configural model). According to Cheung and Rensvold [57], the restricted parameters are invariant between groups if the CFI decreases by less than 0.01. As shown in Table 3, the results established gender invariance of the scale.

We also compared means to clarify if the eight-factor model could differentiate between participants’ scores in terms of gender. Results revealed that there were sig­ nificant gender differences in enjoyment (t(294) = 2.96, d = 0.97, p =.008), hopelessness (t(294)=-2.23, d = 1.05, p =.027), and boredom (t(294)=-2.26, d = 1.14 p =.024) with big effect sizes, while there was no other significant difference in hope, pride, anger, anxiety, and shame. Spe­ cifically, compared to males (M = 2.92, SD = 1.04), females (M = 3.23, SD = 0.92) registered higher mean scores in one positive emotion: enjoyment. In terms of negative emotions, hopelessness was lower for females (M = 2.00, SD = 0.96) than for males (M = 2.28, SD = 1.16), and bore­ dom was also lower for females (M = 2.49, SD = 1.10) than for males (M = 2.79, SD = 1.19) (see Table 4).

Positive emotions, such as enjoyment, hope, and pride, were strongly positively correlated with satis­ faction in life (r =.551, r =.614, and r =.605, respectively, all p <.001), positive affect (r =.837, r = 759, and r =.810, respectively, all p <.001), and team learning satisfaction (r =.650, r =.731, and r =.757, respectively, all p <.001). We futher examined the link between achievement emotions as measured by AEQ-SIPE as a predictor of well-being and team learning satisfaction. The theoreti­ cal link between emotion and well-being [34] and learn­ ing satisfaction [6] has been established previously in other contexts. As shown in Table 6, satisfaction in life (F(8, 295) = 25.499, p <.001, R2 = 0.399), positive affect (F(8, 295) = 107.653, p <.001, R2 = 0.743), negative affect (F(8,295) = 78.429, p <.001, R2 = 0.677), and team learning satisfaction (F(8, 295) = 68.192, p <.001, R2 = 0.646) were significantly predicted by achievement emotions. Specifi­ cally, hope, pride, and shame predicted life satisfaction;

enjoyment, pride, and shame predicted positive affect. These results were consistent with our hypotheses.

Discussion This study aims to determine the construct validity of AEQ-SIPE and advance the conversation on achievement emotions in healthcare education by providing research­ ers with a scale to use in their investigation. The findings supporting the eight-factor structure of the AEQ-SIPE are consistent with previous validation studies, such as the original AEQ-S [21] and its Spanish-translated ver­ sion [17]. The findings further highlight that one can use the short version of the AEQ without sacrificing the structural model of the scale. Our study expands the application of AEQ-S to from individual to collaborative learning environments.

The results of within-network validity revealed that the eight-factor AEQ-S IPE structure obtained a good fit for our current data involving IPE students. Our results met the criteria of acceptable fit using various goodness-offit indices: CFI, NFI, IFI, TLI, RMSEA, and SRMR, sug­ gesting the internal validity of the scale. The results are consistent with previous work supporting AEQ among other samples, such as secondary school students [17] and university students [21]. Our findings reaffirm the factor structure established in prior AEQ validation stud­ ies, confirming the distinctiveness of positive and nega­ tive emotions like pride, enjoyment, shame, and anxiety. The consistency of these constructs across diverse educa­ tional settings highlights the context-independent valid­ ity of the AEQ.

Further, our results showed metric, scalar, configurar invariance providing good support for gender invari­ ance for the AEQ-SIPE eight-factor model. We then per­ formed t-tests to examine gender differences across the eight AEs. Results indicated that females in our sample had significantly higher enjoyment than males, while males were significantly higher in hopelessness and bore­ dom than females. These gender differences in AEs were consistent with the earlier studies in other contexts [19, 61, 62]. One possible reason is that male students are less emotionally invested in and enjoy academic activi­ ties, because they need to develop stronger interpersonal relationships with teachers to become more engaged in learning [63]. In addition, these differences may reflect gendered patterns in traditional gender role expectations and socialization. Traditionally, medicine (a predomi­ nantly male field) has been positioned above nursing and other care professions (predominantly female) in health­ care settings. These contradictory expectations require female students to be assertive and show enjoyment of collaboration to be effective team members. Meanwhile, male students’ higher levels of hopelessness and bore­ dom likely stem from gender socialization that values

On the other hand, we also found some studies that are in contrast with our current findings. For example, a study among physical education students found that males had higher mean scores than females in terms of enjoyment while females had higher mean scores than males in terms of hopelessness and boredom [65]. In addition, a study among English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners also found that males had higher enjoy­ ment mean scores than females and females had higher hopelessness mean scores than males. In our results in the IPE context, one possible explanation is that per­ ceived gender norms can play a role on how Chinese students express their academic engagement and motiva­ tion [66, 67], and academic commitment [68]. Altogether, contrasting findings seem to exist in the literature regard­ ing gender differences in achievement emotions and our present findings add to this existing debate.

To establish the between-network validity, we con­ ducted correlation and regression analyses, which revealed a significant relationship between AEs and sub­ sequent well-being (life satisfaction and affect) and learn­ ing satisfaction. For example, pride positively predicted life satisfaction, positive affect, and learning satisfaction, while shame negatively predicted life satisfaction but pos­ itively predicted positive affect and negative affect. These findings are in general alignment with earlier studies [20, 69]. However, we also found non-significant relationships between some emotions and well-being and learning sat­ isfaction (e.g., anxiety and team learning satisfaction).

These non-significant results suggest that some emo­ tions may not directly impact well-being or learning satisfaction but could act through other mediators or moderators For example, previous study was found that the relationship between achievement emotions and aca­ demic achievement was moderated by academic buoy­ ancy [70]. Future research could explore these indirect pathways or environmental factors to gain a more com­ prehensive understanding of the role of emotions in education. Moreover, a counterintuitive finding of this study relates to boredom and shame, where contrary to our prediction, boredom positively predicted team learn­ ing satisfaction, and shame positively predicted positive affect. While we are surprised that this result requires further investigation, this may be explained by the speci­ fied beneficial effects of boredom or its different types [71] in some individuals under specific circumstances [72]. In IPE settings, boredom might serve a produc­ tive function by providing mental space for students to process complex interprofessional interactions, offering necessary mental breaks during intensive collaborative sessions where cognitive overload is common. Previous studies have suggested that boredom might not always directly enhance learning strategies [73], but can some­ times encourage individuals to seek new goals and expe­ riences [74]. Similarly, the positive correlation between shame and positive affect may appear unexpected. This relationship may reflect the distinctive learning dynam­ ics of IPE, where shame experienced after recognizing knowledge gaps about other professions’ roles can trigger heightened engagement and motivation to improve col­ laborative competencies. In healthcare education where professional identity formation is closely tied to com­ petency development, shame may function as a catalyst for professional growth when experienced in supportive interprofessional environments. Research indicates that certain negative emotions, like shame, can sometimes contribute to positive outcomes if they motivate individ­ uals to improve their performance or engage more deeply with the content to avoid future negative feelings [75]. Our initial results on the relationship between shame and outcomes require further investigation.

Limitations Although this study has merits, it also has limitations that open up new research directions. First, although self-report measures are frequently used to collect data for confirmatory research due to their ease of use and data collection efficiency, this restriction raises the possibility of method bias [77]. Future studies could incorporate multiple data sources, such as behavioral observations to triangulate findings and enhance validity. Second, although eight different disciplines were included in the study, the sampling area was only in Hong Kong, and the sample size was not very large. Additionally, due to the challenges in participant recruitment result­ ing in the unbalanced distribution of participants across healthcare disciplines, with medical and nursing students comprising 73% of the sample while some disciplines had minimal representation (engineering n = 2, speech and hearing sciences n = 4), may limit the generalizability of findings across all healthcare fields. The smaller sample sizes in certain disciplines preclude meaningful subgroup analyses and may not fully capture discipline-specific achievement emotion patterns. Given that medical and nursing programs typically involve high-intensity clini­ cal training, the current findings may be most represen­ tative of achievement emotions in intensive healthcare education contexts. Future research would benefit from more balanced recruitment across healthcare disciplines

Conclusion By and large, we are excited about the newly validated AEQ-SIPE, as this signals a great opportunity for health professional education researchers to contribute to mov­ ing the healthcare education literature forward. Theoreti­ cally, this study provides researchers with the impetus to investigate the relationship between subjective feel­ ings and other variables in the setting of IPE. There­ fore, we propose utilizing AEQ-SIPE to develop mean­ ingful research agendas in IPE.

**Affiliations:** aCritical Care Medicine Unit, School of Clinical Medicine, LKS Faculty of Medicine, The University of Hong Kong, Pok Fu Lam, Hong Kong Island, HKSAR | bBau Institute of Medical and Health Sciences Education, LKS Faculty of Medicine, The University of Hong Kong, Pok Fu Lam, Hong Kong Island, HKSAR | cHKU Health System Clinical Center, LKS Faculty of Medicine, The University of Hong Kong, Pok Fu Lam, Hong Kong Island, HKSAR

## Abstract

Simulation-based training (SBT) is an integral and indispensable component of medical and healthcare education, especially pertinent in acute care. Conventional forms of SBT in acute care primarily involve manikins or task trainers, which are either costly or too task-specific. Recent innovations in virtual patient simulation software (VPS) invites the opportunity for conjoined use with basic manikins, creating a hybrid model for acute-care teaching. This study aimed to: ① Assess the impact of hybrid simulation teaching on the collective efficacy (CE) and self-efficacy (SE) of medical students, and ② evaluate psychometric measurement scales within the simulation context.

A prospective cross-sectional cohort study was conducted between 22 September 2023, and 19 December 2023. Fifth year medical students in an undergraduate medicine program underwent hybrid SBT, incorporating VPS and basic manikin within two separate clinical scenarios. Primary outcome of CE and SE was measured using adapted versions of the Perceived Collective Efficacy (PCE) scale and Motivational Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ). Both scales were distributed to students before and after undergoing hybrid SBT.

Data from 94 students were available for pairwise testing. Significant improvements were observed in the CE and SE of students after undergoing hybrid SBT [CE: (12.16 ± 3.86 vs 15.42 ± 2.87); p < 0.001]; [SE: 24(23–32) vs 32(28–34); p < 0.001]. Scale evaluation of Perceived Collective Efficacy (PCE) and Motivational Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) revealed good scale Cronbach α scores [PCE: pretest α = 0.929; posttest α = 0.914]; [MSLQ: pretest α = 0.971.; posttest α = 0.968].

Hybrid SBT facilitated by virtual patient simulator and basic manikin provides a moderate-cost and adaptable approach which positively impacted the CE and SE of medical students. As software development readily adapts in providing point-of-care learner feedback, hybrid SBT should become more widely implemented to fully harness its potential.

## Introduction

Since the revolutionary inception of the Resusci Anne and the Harvey Simulator in the 1960s, simulation-based training (SBT) has become an integral and indispensable component of healthcare education [1–7]. At its core, continued prevalence of SBT in modern healthcare is attributed to its effectiveness in providing hands-on experience to students without compromising patient care, providing learners a risk-free platform for repeated practices in safe and controlled environments [1–3]. These simulators have laid the foundation for training in healthcare practices, everchanging to meet the dynamic needs of the industry. Notable instances of dynamic adaptations include standardized simulation training modality incorporating basic manikin with simulated patient scenarios, like those seen in procedural protocols including basic life support (BLS) and advanced cardiovascular support (ACLS).

As of current, a variety of simulator modalities are implemented within medical and healthcare education [1,2,8–13], including manikin simulators, task trainers, virtual reality and standardized patients. With a wide array of simulators to pick and choose from, a pressing dilemma is presented: ‘How can we effectively consolidate the complex management of a patient into one intricate bundle?’. This is where hybrid SBT models become pertinent, offering unique properties that offset the limitations posed by singular model approach. The hybrid model we posit in this study includes a combination of basic task trainer manikin and virtual patient simulation (VPS) in a cohort of Asian medical students.

When designing SBT, one concept that often emerges is that of fidelity. In the context of our study, fidelity is defined according to Hamstra et al. which stratifies fidelity into two dimensions: (i) physical resemblance – characterized by the tactile, visual, auditory and olfactory appearance of the simulator relative to the simulation concept in mind; and (ii) functional task alignment – the simulator’s functional property in alignment with the learning objectives at hand [5,14–16].

This distinction is crucial in defining the proposed hybrid SBT model, as unequivocal interpretations of ‘high-fidelity’ in wider literature complicate model selection, particularly in resource-limited settings [8–13]. For instance, while a ‘high-fidelity’ manikin realistically simulating the physical resemblance and haemodynamics of a patient may be desirable, they often incur high costs, require extensive preparation and lack flexibility in scenario adaptation [15–18]. Conversely, ‘low-fidelity’ basic manikins including those used in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) training may not realistically depict the physical appearance of a patient, but can just as effectively facilitate functional alignment with tasks expected in CPR training (e.g. compression rhythm and timing mastery) at much lower costs and requirements in trainer preparation [19,20]. Furthermore, by incorporating elements of VPS into a model with basic task trainer manikin, we potentiate effects of both modalities by generating a logistically sound and feasible platform with elements of psychological benefits of enhanced engagement through the incorporation of immediate feedback and student tailoring.

Other drawbacks of high-fidelity manikin simulation include the need for extra staff to operate control panels and the additional training needed to respond and adapt to unexpected learner decisions. Furthermore, high-fidelity simulation also incurs high costs ranging from equipment, extra personnel and time required to train the trainer. Our proposed hybrid SBT model aims to enhance task-alignment of a standalone ‘low-fidelity’ CPR manikin by incorporating interactive elements seen in VPS, of which comes pre-programmed with patient scenarios and emulated haemodynamics. In doing so, this substitutes physical exam findings and other clinical information to be relayed through a high-fidelity manikin. The result is an adaptable, cost effective and effort efficient model alternative to conventional standalone high-fidelity manikin (Supplement S1) [21,22]. It is for these positive qualities and the team-based environment that hybrid SBT fosters which warrants further investigation.

To our knowledge, literature surrounding the combination of virtual-based education and traditional manikin-based training has not been extensively researched in the context of medical students, particularly with their effects on collective and self-efficacy. Despite the lower costs, versatility and Extant literature have mostly explored standalone modalities (e.g. VPS or ‘High-fidelity’ manikins) with respect to learner knowledge, competency, or during clinical examinations [1,2,6,7,14]. However, hybrid modalities (or ‘medium fidelity’ simulations) and their effects on CE and SE within Asian medical students have not been thoroughly examined. As such, we hypothesize that a hybrid learning modality combining VPS and basic task trainer manikins can positively impact CE and SE in medical students much the same way that ‘high-fidelity’ simulator modalities can in the context of acute patient care.

In light of these knowledge gaps, the aims and objectives of our study were to therefore: ① Evaluate the effects of hybrid SBT on the CE and SE of clinical year medical students; and ② validate scales for use in measuring collective and self-efficacy in the context of medical simulation education.

## Materials and methods

This study aimed to explore the impact of hybrid SBT on the CE and SE of fifth-year medical students at the University of Hong Kong. A cross-sectional cohort design was employed, conducted during the first semester of the 2023–2024 academic year, with students enrolled in mandatory critical care simulation sessions. Ethical approval for the study was granted by the HKU/HA HKW Institutional Review Board (IRB) in September 2023 (Reference number UW23-410). The following sections outline the study design, participant recruitment, data collection procedures and data analysis methods used to investigate the effects of hybrid SBT on student’s CE and SE.

### Study design and setting

Hybrid SBT was first implemented into the medical curricula. In the local study setting of Hong Kong, the first semester comprises the months of September to December. We opted for a cross-sectional cohort design as we aimed to recruit as many participants as possible to adequately power our study for hypothesis generation. The design choice was appropriate in evaluating changes in CE and SE arising immediately from the hybrid simulation model. Furthermore, as we did not provide any incentives for the participants, a cross-sectional design would eliminate attrition issues conventionally seen in longitudinal studies.

The fifth-year medical students sampled within our study are representative of medical students in the middle of their clinical clerkships, both locally and beyond Hong Kong. As such, all fifth-year medical students rotating through their ICU clerkships were approached and offered recruitment during the first semester. This study took place 22 September and 19 December 2023, at The University of Hong Kong. All participants were provided two separate informed consent sheets on the pre- and post-tests through written or digital means.

Inclusion criteria were ① all fifth-year undergraduate medical students, ② rotating through their ICU clerkship who, ③ consented to participation. As part of curriculum renewal efforts, all fifth-year medical students at the institution were the first cohort to participate in a newly established mandatory critical care simulation program during the 2023–2024 semester. This cohort was therefore selected through convenience sampling on practical grounds.

Exclusion criteria were fifth-year medical students who were involved in the pilot trials of the SBT, students with missing data from either the pre- or post SBT survey, and students who arrived late for the SBT. The study key criterion for missing data included either missing pre- or post-test scores. As the participant identification was dependent on de-identified self-reported initials, matching pre- and post- results depended on consistent reporting of student initials. Late participants also increased the margin for missing data, as the concurrent scheduling of the study with SBT sessions would cause them to miss the pretest but maintain eligibility to consent for the post-test. The full trial protocol is enclosed within Appendix 1.

### Study conceptual framework

Traditionally, research on SBT within medical education has heavily emphasized clinical skills, problem-based learning, or academic excellence as outcomes of interest [1,2,13]. While these performative domains certainly do serve as predictive outcomes on academic performance [13], burgeoning strides are being made towards the induction of alternative, holistic learning attitudes into learner. Some notable instances of these learning attitudes include collective efficacy (CE) and self-efficacy (SE) [23–28], both of which emerge from and play a central theme in Bandura’s Self-Efficacy Theory (1997) and Social Cognitive Theory (2001).

To elucidate further, CE is an emergent group property resulting from the efforts of a team rather than from a single individual. CE represents a group’s shared belief in their conjoint efforts to organize and execute courses of actions required to accomplish specific tasks, rather than each individual [29–31]. Previous studies report improved CE being linked with key psychological outcomes, including increased levels of team effort, improved perseverance in face of adversity and increased motivation. Attitudes such as motivation are posited to increase due to belief that individuals within a team have little incentive to act unless they perceive their actions to produce desirable results [23,31–34]. Consequently, it is the sum of these behaviours and attitudes that predict future performance in a group-based healthcare setting [23,24,32,33], subsequently translating into positive clinical outcomes including reduction in clinical near misses, improved patient outcomes and fostering constructive communication between peers [23,34].

Analogous to CE is its individualistic counterpart SE. Distinctively, SE emphasizes on an individual’s belief in themselves to organize and execute actions to achieve attainment in specific tasks [29,30,35,36]. Furthermore, SE should also be distinguished from other similar concepts like self-esteem and self-confidence, as SE is more context-dependent and strongly associated with future performance. In contrast, self-esteem and self-confidence present as broader and generalized behaviours that do not directly associate with future performance [26,29]. Much like CE, higher levels of SE attainment are associated with salubrious outcomes within an individual, including learning engagement, increased motivation and academic success among medical students [27–29,37,38]. There are posited to be several sources of stimuli inducted into learners that drive attitudinal behaviours and elicit positive outcomes when performing specific tasks. These sources include verbal persuasion, vicarious experiences, emotional arousal and task accomplishment [29,35,36].

Relevant instances of stimuli being applied into practice include standardized life support algorithms like Basic Life Support. BLS programs offer learners the opportunity to freely practice fundamental lifesaving skills in high-stake and controlled environments. By repeatedly practicing compressions in these simulated environments, learners gradually buildup mastery experiences through repeated task accomplishments. This study hopes to extend the abovementioned frameworks onto hybrid SBT, demonstrating it an adequate driver for instilling mastery experiences and vicarious experiences onto students.

### Study materials

The setup for hybrid SBT included a simple bedside environment with one basic CPR manikin and an interactive display monitor (Figure 2). The display was used to project the VPS software, BodyInteract™, which students were able to interact through. Teaching case scenarios were selected based on availability within the software, supplemented with the manikin. We selected cases based on clinical competencies expected of a fifth-year medical student within the institution. Additional equipment used in both scenarios included simple airway devices (e.g. nasal cannula and non-rebreather masks), haemodynamic monitoring devices (e.g. blood pressure machines), mock intravenous medications and cannulations (e.g. central lines).

The first case presented a patient with an intracranial haemorrhage to address the systematic approach in assessing an unconscious patient. Key learning objectives from the scenario were ① assessment recognition of an unstable patient via a systematic ABCDE (airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure) approach, ② differential diagnosis of unconsciousness and ③ basic airway management (e.g. use of nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal airway adjuncts). This case was selected as first in order according to the simpler management expected from students.

The second case featured a patient with sepsis secondary to pneumonia, which aimed to address the systematic approach in assessing and managing a patient with sepsis. Key learning objectives from second case were ① identification and diagnosis of septic shock, ② implementation and resuscitation of the virtual patient through the sepsis-1-hour bundle according to the surviving sepsis campaign guidelines [39]. This case scenario was selected due to the prevalence of the disease pathology within critical care and also due to the increased complexity to offset for potential baseline advantages gained in the observer role during the first scenario. After cycling through both were roughly 10 min long and aimed to reinforce the key learning objectives of the case, and address any management plans the students may have overlooked.

As we aimed to better deduce the learning affects of students, the teaching clinician and simulation facilitator would purposively foster a mastery-oriented climate where participants would be encouraged cooperate among peers, reinforce personal goal improvements and emphasize mistake-making as part of the process in our controlled hybrid SBT environment. Consequently, we did not seek to proactively assess or grade student competency or performance for the intents of the study. We ascertained that in acute-care practice, a predominantly performance-oriented motivational climate would result in intra-team member rivalry, unequal recognition among peers and undermine psychological safety of participants in fear of reprimand for speaking up [40–43], traits of which we perceive as detrimental in team-based approaches during acute-care management.

Each SBT session included 10 students. Five medical students would actively participate in team-based management, whereas the other five students would observe and record actions undertaken by the participating team. Two members of staff were actively engaged in SBT, including a teaching clinician and a simulation facilitator. Main roles and responsibilities of the teaching clinician included delivering key learning objectives and providing post-scenario debriefs. The clinician would adopt a situational leadership approach [44], offering students direction and guidance as needed.

The simulation facilitator was responsible for bridging the gap between the manikin and VPS. They would mirror physical exams performed on the manikin to the VPS and select management plans on the VPS based on group decisions. The results of student actions are relayed as real-time feedback on the VPS, such as the virtual patient’s condition improving or deteriorating based on the adequacy of treatment provided. All staff involved received brief training on the VPS and scenarios prior to the sessions, which is supplemented by a tutor guide (See Appendix 2a, 2b and 2c in the Supplement). Development of simulation-based scenarios were based on Kolb’s experimental learning theory [45], covering aspects of concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization and active experimentation. The surveys scales used were reviewed by two independent content experts for relevance to scenario content and learning objectives.

### Measurement tools

#### Collective efficacy (CE)

CE was measured using the four-item Perceived Collective Efficacy (PCE) Likert scale, adapted from the General Self Efficacy Scale developed by Schwarzer (1995) [46] and modified by Salanova [47] for work groups. This scale has been validated in cohorts of Hong Kong undergraduate and medical students [23,46]. It is due to this previous validation in a similar cohort that we have subsequently adapted the PCE items to our hybrid SBT context to more accurately measure CE in acute/critical care settings. For instance, the original item, ‘My group is able to solve difficult tasks if we invest the necessary effort’, was adapted to ‘My group is able to manage a critically ill patient if we invest the necessary effort’. Responses were scored on a five-point Likert scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

#### Self-efficacy (SE)

Measurements for SE were conducted using an eight-item adapted subscale based on the original Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) SE for learning and performance subscale [48,49]. MSLQ has been previously validated and used in measuring SE of Western and Asian medical students in problem-based learning environments [50,51]. We have subsequently adapted the MSLQ’s self-efficacy for learning and performance subscale items to our hybrid SBT context to more accurately measure SE in acute/critical care settings. For example, the item from the original self-efficacy for learning and performance subscale, ‘I am confident I can understand the basic concepts taught in this course’, was adapted to ‘I am confident I can/will understand the basic concepts in the explored topic areas (e.g. managing critically ill patients’. Each item was scored on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

#### Subgroup measures

Sub-group analysis of differences between male and female were conducted with the rationale of uncovering underlying social dynamics between differences in gender and their respective effects on student CE/SE expectations within simulation [52]. Better understanding gender dynamics and social influences on CE/SE will aid in establishing learner centred teaching approaches.

As the medical syllabus within the local context was offered as an undergraduate route, differences in undergraduates vs postgraduates were also selected as a sub-group of interest. We sought to determine whether mature postgraduate students would attain higher CE/SE scores compared to their undergraduate counterparts at baseline and after completing hybrid SBT.

#### Secondary outcome

Secondary outcome measures to evaluate the adapted CE and SE scales in the context of SBT were defined according to the recommendations proposed by Boateng et al. and Dima [53,54]. Boateng et al. posits that scale development and validation are split into three phases of item development, scale development and scale evaluation. For the purposes of this study, we aimed to evaluate preexisting scales in the context of our study population and hybrid SBT activity. To achieve this, we conducted confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) of a single-factor model. Because latent variables such as CE and SE cannot be tangibly observed, measurements of these variables become implausible. Therefore, strategies are needed operationally define latent variables such that they can represent a behaviour or outcome of interest. It is for this reason that CFA is important, as it determines scale validity by psychometrically testing the systematic fit of a specified model by determining the relationship between observable variables (e.g. items within the scale) and latent constructs (e.g. collective efficacy). In doing so, we ensure our scale accurately and appropriately measures the intended latent construct, thus enabling us to draw reliable conclusions on the effect of intervention through data [23,55,56]. Since the scales we adapted for use had already been previously validated in a cohort of medical students in Hong Kong [23,24], we did not allocate items of the scale to be freely estimated as expected in exploratory factor analysis, and sought only to ascertain if data we collected fit the a priori model. Scale evaluation was therefore divided into two sections: ① Tests of dimensionality – measured CFA; and ② Tests of reliability – measured through Cronbach’s α.

### Data analysis

Student demographics were summarized using descriptive statistics. Categorical data was presented as frequencies with percentages. Normally distributed continuous variables were presented as means with standard deviations, whereas non-normally distributed continuous variables were depicted and expressed as medians with interquartile ranges. To justify the sample size for our study cohort, we obtained preliminary data from a pilot trial involving 18 volunteer fifth-year medical students. As these students would undergo the same interventions and stimuli, they would be excluded from the main study. Paired continuous variables were obtained, with the mean differences and standard deviations used to calculate preliminary effect and sample size. Assuming an α error of 0.05 and 1-β error of 0.8, preliminary effect sizes obtained in the pilot CE and SE results were d = 0.636 and d = 0.919 respectively, indicating an estimated sample size of at least n = 22 for detecting a statistically significant difference in CE and n = 12 in SE.

Shapiro-Wilk (SW) tests were used to assess data distribution [57,58]. Pre- and post-test CE scores were normally distributed, therefore paired samples t-tests were used for CE analysis. Underlying assumptions for t-tests SE pretest scores were non-normally distributed, therefore necessitating Wilcoxon Signed-Rank tests for analysis (Supplement S2). The Wilcoxon Signed-Rank tests are for paired and non-normally distributed data that assumes independence between pairs and symmetrical distribution of differences between groups. Box-and-whisker plots would be used to visually display the median (Q2), lower quartile (Q1), third quartile (Q3) and outliers for CE and SE scores of the primary outcome. Effect sizes of normally distributed results were reported using Cohen’s d while effect sizes of non-normally distributed results were reported using rank biserial correlation, a simple difference formula used in computing effect sizes for Mann Whitney U in providing insight into correlations [59].

Exploratory sub-group analyses of gender differences and undergraduate vs postgraduate differences were conducted using independent two-samples t-tests for normally distributed continuous variables, and Mann-Whitney U tests for non-normally distributed continuous variables (Supplement S3). Mann-Whitney U tests are for non-normally distributed data that are independent of each other between groups, the assumption of symmetrical distribution of differences still hold [60].

The assumptions of confirmatory factory analyses are correct model specification, random sampling, adequate sample size, multivariate normal distribution and linearity between observed and latent variables. Cronbach’s α analyses measure how closely related and consistent a set of survey items are by comparing the amount of shared variance. Data management and statistical analysis were conducted using Stata-18 software (StataCorp LP), with a two-tailed statistical significance of p < 0.05 [61].

For our secondary outcome of validating scale acceptability, we conducted CFA [53,54] to assess and determine the suitability of our adapted scale and the original a priori factor structures in our current sample. Results from CFA include chi-square test of exact fit, degrees of freedom, root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA ≤ 0.06), Tucker Lewis Index (TLI ≥ 0.95), comparative fit index (CFI ≥ 0.95) and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR ≤ 0.08) [53,62]. Reliability tests were performed using Cronbach’s α in both CE and SE scales in pretest and posttest, as well as the Corrected item-total correlations and Cronbach’s α if item is deleted. Statistical analysis of secondary outcomes were performed on IBM SPSS Statistics Version 29.0.2.0 [63] and IBM SPSS AMOS 28 Graphics for scale validation [64]. All p values obtained were two-tailed, with values less than 0.05 indicating statistical significance.

## Results

The purpose of this study was to examine the impact of hybrid SBT on CE and SE among fifth-year medical students. Results from the analysis are presented below, starting with primary outcomes, followed by subgroup analyses, secondary outcomes and participant feedback.

### Primary outcome

#### Impact of hybrid SBT on CE and SE

In our primary outcome, CE scores were paired and normally distributed. Therefore, paired t-tests were employed, with effect sizes reported as Cohen’s d. For analysis of paired independent non-normally distributed SE scores, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Tests were employed for, with effect size reported using rank biserial correlations.

Students reported significantly lower CE scores at baseline as compared to posttest. However, after progressing through hybrid SBT their CE scores significantly increased, which is further evidenced by means and standard deviations of their pretest vs posttest CE scores (12.16 ± 3.859 vs 15.42 ± 2.87, p < 0.001) Large effect size (d = 0.811) suggests that the improvements are of practical significance after undergoing hybrid SBT.

A similar trend was observed in the SE of students, where their self-perceived SE at baseline was significantly lower, but would subsequently be improved after undergoing hybrid SBT as evidenced by the median of their pretest vs posttest SE scores (24, 23–32, vs 32, 28–34, p < 0.001). A medium to moderate effect size (rpb = 0.461) suggests that differences were practical and substantial after undergoing hybrid SBT. Detailed test results are shown in Tables 2 and 3 and Figure 4.

### Subgroup analyses

#### Gender differences in CE and SE
